title: Text surgery
summary: Marketing's customer export is a crime scene: semicolons, stray spaces, SHOUTING emails, Windows line endings and duplicates. Operate with tr, sed, cut, sort, uniq and awk.

nodes.garibaldi: the reporting server; the export is /srv/export/customers.csv

tasks.title: Invisible carriage returns
tasks.text: Look at the patient: `head -5 /srv/export/customers.csv`, then `head -3 /srv/export/customers.csv | cat -A` (`-A` makes invisible characters visible). Every line ends in `^M$`: Windows line endings (`\r\n`), which confuse Linux tools. Write a copy without them to `/root/step1.csv`.

checks.fail_msg: /root/step1.csv does not exist yet (or is empty).
step1.csv should have the same number of lines as the original.

hints: `tr` translates or deletes characters. `tr -d 'x'` deletes every x. It reads stdin only, so feed it with `<`.
`tr -d '\r' < /srv/export/customers.csv > /root/step1.csv`. (`sed 's/\r$//'` works too, and so does `dos2unix` where it is installed.)

tasks.title: Head count
tasks.text: How many customer **rows** say they live in **{{CITY}}**? City names are messy (`YORK`, ` York `, `york`), so count them all. Count rows as they are, duplicates included, and don't count the header.

answer_cmd.cmd: tr -d '\r' < /srv/export/customers.csv | tail -n +2 | awk -F';' '{c = $4; gsub(/ /, "", c); if (tolower(c) == "{{CITY}}") n++} END {print n + 0}'

hints: Fields are separated by `;`. `cut -d';' -f4 /root/step1.csv` prints the city column.
Make the column uniform before counting: `tr -d ' '` removes spaces and `tr 'A-Z' 'a-z'` lowercases.
`tail -n +2 /root/step1.csv | cut -d';' -f4 | tr -d ' ' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sort | uniq -c` counts every city at once.

answer_cmd.cmd: tr -d '\r' < /srv/export/customers.csv | tail -n +2 | cut -d';' -f4 | tr -d ' ' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | grep -cx '{{CITY}}'

tasks.title: Stitch it into a clean CSV
tasks.text: Make `/root/clean.csv`: the same rows **without the header**, fields separated by **commas**, spaces at the start and end of every field removed (keep the space inside a name like `Ada Lovelace`), and the **email** and **city** in lowercase. A row should look like `317,Ada Lovelace,ada.lovelace@example.com,leeds,12`.

checks.fail_msg: /root/clean.csv does not exist yet (or is empty).
The header line is still there.

checks.cmd: diff <(tr -d '\r' < /srv/export/customers.csv | tail -n +2 | awk -F';' -v OFS=, '{for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) gsub(/^ +| +$/, "", $i); $3 = tolower($3); $4 = tolower($4); print}') /root/clean.csv > /dev/null
checks.fail_msg: Not quite the expected rows yet. Compare a few lines of your file with the example: commas, no stray spaces, lowercase email and city, same row order as the original.

hints: Build it one stage at a time: `tail -n +2` drops the header, then trim, then lowercase, then swap `;` for `,`.
`sed 's/ *; */,/g'` turns `;` plus any spaces around it into a single comma; `sed 's/^ *//; s/ *$//'` trims the ends of the line.
Lowercasing only two columns is a job for awk: `awk -F, -v OFS=, '{ $3 = tolower($3); $4 = tolower($4); print }'`. (`-F` is the input separator, `OFS` the output one.)
All together: `tail -n +2 /root/step1.csv | sed 's/ *; */,/g; s/^ *//; s/ *$//' | awk -F, -v OFS=, '{ $3 = tolower($3); $4 = tolower($4); print }' > /root/clean.csv`

steps.cmd: tail -n +2 /root/step1.csv | sed 's/ *; */,/g; s/^ *//; s/ *$//' | awk -F, -v OFS=, '{ $3 = tolower($3); $4 = tolower($4); print }' > /root/clean.csv

tasks.title: Seeing double
tasks.text: Some customers were exported twice. Make `/root/unique.csv`: `clean.csv` with every row appearing **once**, sorted by **ID** numerically (smallest first).

checks.fail_msg: /root/unique.csv does not exist yet (or is empty).

checks.cmd: diff <(tr -d '\r' < /srv/export/customers.csv | tail -n +2 | awk -F';' -v OFS=, '{for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) gsub(/^ +| +$/, "", $i); $3 = tolower($3); $4 = tolower($4); print}' | sort -t, -k1,1n | uniq) /root/unique.csv > /dev/null
checks.fail_msg: unique.csv should be clean.csv's rows, each once, sorted numerically by the first column.

hints: `sort` puts identical lines next to each other; `uniq` then drops the repeats. `sort -u` does both.
Numeric sort on the first comma-separated field: `sort -t, -k1,1n` (`-t,` separator, `-k1,1` field 1 only, `n` numeric). So: `sort -t, -k1,1n /root/clean.csv | uniq > /root/unique.csv`.

tasks.title: Customer of the year
tasks.text: Marketing wants to send a giant golden biscuit to the customer with the **most orders** (last column). What is their email address?

answer_cmd.cmd: tr -d '\r' < /srv/export/customers.csv | tail -n +2 | awk -F';' -v OFS=, '{for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) gsub(/^ +| +$/, "", $i); $3 = tolower($3); $4 = tolower($4); print}' | sort -t, -k1,1n | uniq | sort -t, -k5,5nr | head -1 | cut -d, -f3

hints: Sort `unique.csv` on field 5, numerically, biggest first: `sort -t, -k5,5nr /root/unique.csv | head -3`.
Then `cut -d, -f3` keeps only the email. Or in awk: `awk -F, '$5 > max { max = $5; who = $3 } END { print who }' /root/unique.csv`.

answer_cmd.cmd: awk -F, '$5 > max { max = $5; who = $3 } END { print who }' /root/unique.csv

tasks.title: The report Brenda actually wants
tasks.text: From `unique.csv`, write `/root/report.txt` with **one line per city**: the city and its **total orders** (sum of the last column), separated by a space, biggest total first. For example `leeds 214`.

checks.fail_msg: /root/report.txt does not exist yet (or is empty).

checks.cmd: [ "$(tr -d '\r' < /srv/export/customers.csv | tail -n +2 | awk -F';' -v OFS=, '{for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) gsub(/^ +| +$/, "", $i); $3 = tolower($3); $4 = tolower($4); print}' | sort -t, -k1,1n | uniq | awk -F, '{t[$4] += $5} END {for (c in t) print c, t[c]}' | sort -k2,2nr)" = "$(awk '{print $1, $2}' /root/report.txt)" ]
checks.fail_msg: Not the expected report: one line per city as `city total`, totals from unique.csv (no duplicates), biggest first.

hints: Summing per group is awk's party trick: an **associative array** keyed by city. `t[$4] += $5` adds each row's orders to its city's total.
Print the totals at the END: `awk -F, '{ t[$4] += $5 } END { for (c in t) print c, t[c] }' /root/unique.csv`. The order is random...
...so sort it on the second field, numerically, reversed: `... | sort -k2,2nr > /root/report.txt`.

steps.cmd: awk -F, '{ t[$4] += $5 } END { for (c in t) print c, t[c] }' /root/unique.csv | sort -k2,2nr > /root/report.txt
